_what_this_is: Every tool BrowserAI knows of, and whether it forwards a call naming one. A tool absent from this file is a tool nobody has judged: a call naming it is refused at the BrowserAI door and never reaches Playwright. Regenerating the tools/list snapshot does NOT update this file -- that is the point.
_stop_before_you_edit_this_file: UPSTREAM-REVIEW.md. Adding a row is adopting a tool, and a row removed is a capability withdrawn.
_the_three_verdicts: allow -- forwarded to the child of the session it names, byte-identical. deny -- refused at the door AND kept out of tools/list entirely; carries why (the refusal a caller reads) and since (when it was judged). *Corrected 2026-10-04 (previously the why was the refusal a caller reads, as this sentence still says): a call naming a denied tool now gets the answer a call naming a tool BrowserAI does not have gets, and the why is the record of the judgement.* answer -- BrowserAI answers it itself. *Corrected 2026-09-21 (previously "answer -- BrowserAI answers it itself; it never had a child to reach").* Seven of the eight never had a child to reach and browserai_page_tool does: it resolves a name against the session child's live tool list and forwards a tools/call to it. What makes it an answer row rather than an allow row is whose tool it is -- it is BrowserAI's, it is advertised from SessionToolSurface.Names, and the door does not judge it, because being in that list IS the judgement. *Corrected 2026-10-08 (previously "Seven of the eight"): eight of the nine never had a child to reach, since browserai_close joined them by the maintainer's decision F1 a; browserai_close reaches its session's child only as BrowserAI's own close, which no verdict is asked about.*
_rows_removed_because_upstream_withdrew_: 2026-09-21, @playwright/mcp 0.0.81 -> 0.0.82. `browser_webmcp_list` (allow, judged 2026-09-15) and `browser_webmcp_call` (deny, judged 2026-09-15) were deleted because upstream marked BOTH `skillOnly: true` in packages/playwright-core/src/tools/backend/webmcp.ts. They keep capability `core` and they are no longer on the wire in ANY configuration: the snapshot's exposed maximum went 74 -> 72 and the default surface 27 -> 25, with skillOnly 9 -> 11. A row naming a tool the snapshot does not carry is a judgement about nothing, which ToolVerdictTests refuses in that direction on purpose. THE DENY'S REASON IS PRESERVED RATHER THAN LOST, because it is the thing a future judgement would need: it was liveness, not security -- `callWebMCPTool` awaits `tab.waitForCompletion` around a page-supplied handler with no timeout, one measured call stood silent for 45 s, and any page can arrange that. RE-READ IN THE 0.0.82 BUNDLE AND STILL TRUE: the new 5 s `kFrameTimeout` bounds the LISTING evaluate per frame and nothing bounds the CALL. So if upstream ever puts these two back on the wire, the deny stands until somebody re-judges it. The reasoning in full is in upstream-review.json under the 2026-09-21 entry.
_an_allow_may_also_carry_why_and_since: Added 2026-09-17 with the first row judged under it. A deny MUST carry both -- the why IS the refusal a caller reads, and nothing else is (*corrected 2026-10-04: no caller reads it since that day, and both are still required, because a deny with no reason is a judgement nobody can re-examine*) -- and an allow that carries them is recording a judgement rather than producing text: why a human looked at this tool and decided a call may pass, and the day they decided. The bare allow rows were judged before this convention and are not wrong; a row with no why is a row whose reasoning is in upstream-review.json instead. Nothing enforces the convention and nothing should: an allow with a manufactured why would be worse than a bare one.
_what_the_answer_rows_actually_do: NOTHING AT RUN TIME, and saying so is the point of this line (added 2026-08-26). The `upstream` half below is load-bearing at the door: ToolVerdicts.Decide reads it on every call and a name with no row is refused. The `authored` half is not. Every browserai_ name skips the verdict door -- seven of the eight are answered before it is reached and browserai_page_tool is let past it explicitly -- and SessionToolSurface.Rewrite advertises the authored tools from SessionToolSurface.Names rather than from this file, so deleting an `answer` row changes nothing a caller can observe. *Corrected 2026-09-21 (previously "SessionToolSurface.IsAuthored short-circuits every browserai_ name BEFORE the verdict door is reached"): browserai_page_tool takes the forwarding path, so it passes the door and is allowed there by being authored rather than by a row.* What these rows ARE is build-and-test-time data: ToolVerdictTests.TheAuthoredRowsAreExactlyTheToolsBrowserAiAnswersItself holds them identical to the authored surface in BOTH directions, so the file and the code cannot drift apart, and Write-ReleaseManifest.ps1 copies the whole file into the release manifest so a rollback can see which tools a build forwarded and which upstream that was judged against. Do not read this as permission to edit them freely: a row here that disagrees with the surface is a red build, which is the whole mechanism. *Corrected 2026-10-08 (previously "seven of the eight are answered before it is reached"): eight of the nine are, since browserai_close joined them.*
_a_note_is_appended_to_the_description: Added 2026-10-04 with the maintainer's rewrite b of the server instructions, in his words: "Rewrite the instructions according to b." An allow row may carry a note: a short piece of BrowserAI advice about that one tool, appended after upstream's own description and marked as BrowserAI's. Upstream's description and schema still come from the child, unchanged. A note on a deny or answer row does not load.
_a_deny_is_answered_like_a_tool_browsera: Since 2026-10-04 a call naming a denied tool gets the same answer as a call naming a tool BrowserAI does not have at all. The why on a deny row is the human record of the judgement, and no model reads it.

browser_close.why: Replaced by BrowserAI's own browserai_close, the maintainer's decision F1 a of 2026-10-08, in his words: "1 b - but think through if browserai_stop and browserai_close could then not just become a single thing." and "f1 a". Playwright's browser_close describes itself as closing the page; in a BrowserAI session it ends the whole browser and its server, and every later call is refused until browserai_resume, which nothing in its name or description says. BrowserAI still sends it to a session's own child for every clean close it makes, the idle close, the shutdown and browserai_close, and the door is never asked about those. A call naming it gets the answer a tool BrowserAI does not have gets, with no text of its own, in his words: "I remember that for the other tools on the deny list we just send the generic \"unknown command\" response and that we do not have tailored answers. If I remember correctly do not make an exception."

browser_resume.why: The reason is liveness. browser_resume releases a call that Playwright's debugger paused and then waits, by upstream's design, for the next pause or for the browser context to close, and in a BrowserAI session neither comes on its own. Measured on @playwright/mcp 0.0.83 with both browser families, 6 runs: the paused call was released within 0.08 s and browser_resume itself had not answered 20 s later; it answered only once the browser closed. BrowserAI puts no timeout on a forwarded call and a call in flight holds off the idle close, so in a headless session the wait lasts until upstream's own one-hour idle timer closes the browser. The released call also does whatever it was asked to do when it was paused, however long ago.

browser_annotate.why: The reason is liveness rather than security: it opens the Playwright Dashboard and waits for a human to draw, it has no self-timeout -- one measured call stood silent for a full 90 s and returned only when its window was closed -- and the window it opens belongs to a SECOND, non-headless browser under a detached daemon that writes outside the session directory. There is no configuration in which it runs headless. An unattended run that called it would hang until it was killed. To see the page, use browser_snapshot for structure or browser_take_screenshot for pixels; both return immediately. If a human really is at the keyboard and has to mark something up, take a screenshot and have them annotate the file.

browser_emulate_media.why: Emulates CSS media features -- prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, forced-colors, prefers-contrast and the print/screen media type -- on the page the session already owns. It reaches nothing outside that page, it returns immediately, and it is the only way to see a site's dark mode or its print stylesheet without a second session. destructiveHint is true because it changes what the page renders, which is the same sense in which browser_navigate is destructive; nothing leaves the profile. Arrived with playwright-core 1.64.0-alpha-2026-09-17 under capability `core`, so it is in upstream's default surface.

browser_network_state_set.note: WARNING -- going offline changes what the page IS, not just what you see. Every request fails as if the network were down, and nothing on screen says you did it, so a human watching a headed window is seeing something you made up. Say so in 'why' and to the human, and set it back online when you are done.

browser_route.note: WARNING -- a route changes what the page IS, not just what you see. A mocked response renders as if the server sent it: the address bar keeps the real origin and nothing on screen says otherwise, so a human watching a headed window is seeing something you made up. Say so in 'why' and to the human, and call browser_unroute when you are done.

browser_take_screenshot.note: 'fullPage: true' leaves at full document height and nothing downscales it: cost follows pixels, with no ceiling. Pass 'filename' for a link to the file and no inline image.

browser_generate_locator.why: BrowserAI drives a browser for tasks and does not write Playwright tests, so the test-writing helpers are not offered. Decided 2026-10-03 by the maintainer, Q365.2 a.

browser_set_storage_state.why: It wipes the profile's cookies and site storage before it loads a saved file, so an old file replaces a newer login, and BrowserAI's profile already keeps logins. Decided 2026-10-04 by the maintainer, Q365.1 a.

browserai_close.why: The ninth authored tool, added by the maintainer's decision F1 a of 2026-10-08: it ends a session's browser and keeps the session, and every later call is refused until browserai_resume. It replaces Playwright's browser_close, which is denied the same day.

browserai_page_tool.why: The eighth authored tool, and the only one that reaches a child: it calls one tool the page under a session's current tab registered with the browser. Since @playwright/mcp 0.0.82 a page can put its own tools on the child's tools/list -- names, descriptions and inputSchemas written by whoever wrote the page -- and deny-by-default refuses every one of them at the door, which is that rule working exactly as designed and which left a real capability unreachable. Page tools are therefore reached as a CLASS, through this one judged tool, rather than through rows: this file is keyed by name and a page's names are unbounded, so a row per page tool is not a thing that can exist. What the class judgement buys back is everything a row would have: the call is bounded by BrowserAI's own timeout, which upstream has none of; the name is re-resolved against the live tab on every call, so a wire name that is a different page's code after a navigation is refused rather than run; the caller's 'why' is recorded on the session like any other call; and 'session' and 'why' never reach the page. A webmcp_* name arriving straight from a client is still refused with no row and no verdict -- this tool does not widen the door, it is the only door.
